notes.front: What is dependency caching in GitHub Actions?
notes.back: Keeping frequently used files, such as downloaded dependencies, in a cache that later workflow runs restore instead of recreating.
notes.explanation: It speeds up recreating files like dependencies that runs would otherwise download each time.
notes.example: Like keeping flour in the cupboard instead of buying a new bag every time you bake.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependency caching”, “About workflow dependency caching”
notes.evidence: To help speed up the time it takes to recreate files like dependencies, {% data variables.product.prodname_dotcom %} can cache files you frequently use in workflows.

notes.front: What is the pool consumption report in Azure Pipelines?
notes.back: A chart, on an agent pool's Analytics tab, of running and queued jobs against your parallel jobs over the previous 30 days.
notes.explanation: It shows whether queued jobs are backing up because running jobs are at the concurrency limit.
notes.example: Like a car park's occupancy log that shows how often every space was full and cars were queuing at the barrier.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure and pay for parallel jobs”, “View job history using the pool consumption report” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can use the **Pool consumption report**, available on the **Analytics** tab of your agent pool, to see a chart of running and queued jobs graphed with your parallel jobs for the previous 30 days.

notes.front: What is a pipeline retention policy in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: A setting that controls how long pipeline runs, classic releases and test data are kept before deletion.
notes.explanation: It balances storage use, compliance and traceability by deciding what is deleted and what is kept longer.
notes.example: Like an office rule to shred receipts after seven years, except the most recent ones and any marked for an audit.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “Retention policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Retention policies control how long pipeline runs, classic releases, and test data are kept in Azure DevOps. These settings help you balance storage usage, compliance, and traceability

notes.front: What is a retention lease on a pipeline run?
notes.back: A lease that extends or controls how long a run is kept, beyond the configured retention period.
notes.explanation: Leases are added or deleted for a run through the Lease API, which a pipeline script can call.
notes.example: Like a library renewal that keeps one book on your shelf past its normal due date.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “Automatically set retention lease on pipeline runs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Retention leases let you extend or control the lifetime of pipeline runs beyond configured retention periods. You can add or delete leases for a pipeline run by using the Lease API.

notes.front: Besides the pass-rate trend, what does the pipeline pass rate report show that helps you cut failures?
notes.back: Which specific task failures contribute most to failed runs, so you can fix the top failing tasks.
notes.explanation: Its sections include a summary, a failure trend per day and the top failing tasks with their failed runs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Pipeline reports”, “Pipeline pass rate report” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can also view which specific task failure contributes to a high number of pipeline run failures, and use that insight to fix the top failing tasks.

notes.front: What does the pipeline duration report measure, and what does it list to help you speed the pipeline up?
notes.back: How long the pipeline typically takes to complete successfully; the top tasks by duration.
notes.explanation: Reviewing the duration trend and the slowest tasks is how the report helps optimise pipeline duration.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Pipeline reports”, “Pipeline duration report” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The **Pipeline duration** report shows how long your pipeline typically takes to complete successfully. You can review the duration trend and analyze the top tasks by duration to optimize the duration of the pipeline.

notes.front: When you turn on flaky test management, what is the default treatment of flaky tests?
notes.back: Flaky tests are used for troubleshooting only; you can instead choose to prevent build failures caused by them.
notes.explanation: You switch the feature on under Project settings > Test management.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage flaky tests”, “Enable flaky test management” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The default setting for all projects is to use flaky tests for troubleshooting.

notes.front: Why do jobs on GitHub-hosted runners gain from dependency caching?
notes.back: They start in a clean runner image and must download dependencies every time, costing network use, runtime and money.
notes.explanation: Tools such as Maven, Gradle, npm and Yarn otherwise rebuild their local dependency cache in each run.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependency caching”, “About workflow dependency caching”
notes.evidence: -hosted runners start in a clean runner image and must download dependencies each time, causing increased network utilization, longer runtime, and increased cost.

notes.front: Caches in GitHub Actions are shared by branch or tag, not by workflow identity. What must you therefore never store in them?
notes.back: Secrets or other sensitive data.
notes.explanation: Any run that can read a cache restores it as-is, so restored files should be treated as untrusted input.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependency caching”, “Cache security”
notes.evidence: Any run that can read a cache restores its contents as-is, so you should treat restored files as untrusted input and never store secrets or other sensitive data in a cache.

notes.front: What does TIA do for a commit it cannot understand?
notes.back: It falls back to running all tests.
notes.explanation: For commits it does understand, it selects impacted, previously failing and newly added tests.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use Test Impact Analysis”, “Speed up testing by using Test Impact Analysis (TIA)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Safe fallback**. For commits and scenarios that TIA can't understand, it falls back to running all tests.

notes.front: What is the documented rule of thumb for how many parallel jobs an organisation needs?
notes.back: About one parallel job for every four to five users.
notes.explanation: Multiple teams, several active branches with continuous integration, or several applications can each call for more.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure and pay for parallel jobs”, “How many parallel jobs do I need?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A simple rule of thumb: Estimate that you need one parallel job for every four to five users in your organization.

notes.front: In the pool consumption report, which pattern suggests buying more parallel jobs?
notes.back: A backlog of queued jobs while running jobs sit at the concurrency limit.
notes.explanation: As queued pipelines outnumber parallel jobs, queues grow longer.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure and pay for parallel jobs”, “View job history using the pool consumption report” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you have a backlog of queued jobs and your running jobs are at the concurrency limit, you might want to purchase more parallel jobs.

notes.front: GitHub Actions runs workflows and jobs concurrently by default; what are two situations the documentation gives for disabling this?
notes.back: Preventing multiple deployments from running at the same time; cancelling linters that check outdated commits.
notes.explanation: Limiting concurrency controls resources when parallel runs could conflict or use more Actions minutes and storage than expected.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Concurrency”, “Concurrency”
notes.evidence: For example, you might want to prevent multiple deployments from running at the same time, or cancel linters checking outdated commits.

notes.front: Can you set a retention policy on an individual pipeline in Azure Pipelines?
notes.back: No. Per-pipeline retention is no longer supported; use project-level retention settings.
notes.explanation: Run retention for YAML and classic build pipelines is set in project settings; classic release pipelines still keep their own release retention.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “Retention policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Pipelines no longer supports per-pipeline retention policies. We recommend that you use project-level retention rules.

notes.front: Under which project settings page do you set retention for runs, artifacts, symbols, attachments and pull request runs?
notes.back: Pipelines > Settings.
notes.explanation: Release retention and test retention have their own pages.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “Configure retention policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Under **Pipelines**, select **Settings** to configure retention for runs, artifacts, symbols, attachments, and pull request runs.

notes.front: Where do you configure how long manual and automated test runs are kept?
notes.back: Project settings > Test > Retention.
notes.explanation: Classic release retention is under Pipelines > Release retention.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “Configure retention policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Under **Test**, select **Retention** to configure how long manual and automated test runs are kept.

notes.front: With Azure Repos, for which branches does "number of recent runs to keep" apply?
notes.back: The pipeline's default branch and each protected branch, plus the pipeline overall.
notes.explanation: A protected branch here is any branch with branch policies; other Git repositories count runs for the whole pipeline.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “Pipeline runs retention policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Azure Repos**: Azure Pipelines retains the configured number of latest runs for the pipeline's default branch and for each protected branch in the repository.

notes.front: Does pipeline run retention delete packages such as NuGet or npm packages?
notes.back: No. It deletes logs, artifacts, symbols, binaries, test results, metadata and source labels or tags, but not packages.
notes.explanation: Packages in feeds follow their own retention settings.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “What parts of the run get deleted” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Pipeline run retention doesn't govern Universal Packages, NuGet, npm, and other packages.

notes.front: A run is past its days limit; what are two other conditions that must also be true before it is deleted?
notes.back: Any two of: not one of the recent runs to keep; not marked for indefinite retention; not retained by a release.
notes.explanation: All the conditions must hold, and retention is processed once a day.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “When are runs deleted” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: - It isn't one of the recent runs as configured in the retention settings. - It isn't marked for indefinite retention. - It isn't retained by a release.

notes.front: Which predefined variables does a pipeline script pass to the Lease API to lease its own run?
notes.back: `runId` and `definitionId`.
notes.explanation: The lease can be for a set duration, shorter for test deployments and longer for production.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “Automatically set retention lease on pipeline runs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can call this API from within a pipeline by using a script and predefined variables for `runId` and `definitionId`.

notes.front: In multistage YAML pipelines, can you set different retention for runs that deploy to a production environment?
notes.back: No. Retention is set only in project settings, not per deployment environment.
notes.explanation: With classic releases you can instead customise retention on the release pipeline.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “How do I specify that runs deployed to production should be retained longer?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you use multistage YAML pipelines, you can configure retention only in project settings. You can't configure retention by deployment environment.

notes.front: To keep build output longer than the retention period, why use the Copy files task rather than Publish build artifacts?
notes.back: Data published as build artifacts is still subject to retention clean-up.
notes.explanation: Copy files puts the output in your own storage location, outside the pipeline's retention.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “Use the Copy files task to save data longer” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Use **Copy files** instead of Publish build artifacts because data published as build artifacts is still subject to retention cleanup.

notes.front: In classic release retention, which wins: the minimum number of releases to keep or the days-based setting?
notes.back: The minimum number of releases.
notes.explanation: The retention timer also resets each time a release is modified or deployed to a stage.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “Releases retention policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The minimum releases setting takes precedence over the days-based setting.

notes.front: What do workflow artifacts let you do once a job has completed?
notes.back: Persist its data and share that data with another job in the same workflow.
notes.explanation: For example, you can keep build and test output after a workflow run has ended.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Workflow artifacts”, “About workflow artifacts”
notes.evidence: Artifacts allow you to persist data after a job has completed, and share that data with another job in the same workflow.

notes.front: How long do deleted packages stay in an Azure Artifacts feed's Recycle Bin, and who can restore them?
notes.back: 30 days; only a feed owner can restore them.
notes.explanation: Feed retention policies can remove older, unpromoted versions automatically as new ones are published.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Artifacts key concepts”, “Retention and the Recycle Bin” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Deleted packages are placed in the Recycle Bin and remain there for 30 days before Azure Artifacts permanently deletes them. Only a feed owner can restore packages from the Recycle Bin.

notes.front: Which Classic pipelines can be exported to YAML?
notes.back: Only those created with the classic build designer; classic release pipelines cannot.
notes.explanation: For a classic release pipeline you export each task individually.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Migrate your Classic pipeline to YAML”, “Migrate your Classic pipeline to YAML” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Only Classic pipelines created using the classic build designer can be exported a YAML.

notes.front: After pasting an exported Classic pipeline into YAML, what must you check about its scheduled triggers?
notes.back: The cron schedules: YAML uses Coordinated Universal Time by default, Classic used the organisation's time zone.
notes.explanation: Variables defined in the Classic editor also have to be redefined in the YAML file or pipeline settings.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Migrate your Classic pipeline to YAML”, “Update your YAML pipeline” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: YAML schedules use UTC by default, while Classic pipelines use your organization’s local time zone.

notes.front: Why does Microsoft recommend YAML pipelines instead of Classic pipelines for security?
notes.back: For added security and fewer accidental misconfigurations, avoiding the risk of YAML and Classic pipelines sharing resources.
notes.explanation: YAML pipelines are code, so they gain code review, branch policies and approvals and checks.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Secure your Azure Pipelines”, “Use YAML pipelines instead of Classic pipelines” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For added security and to reduce the risk of accidental misconfigurations, use YAML pipelines instead of Classic pipelines. This precaution prevents a security concern arising from YAML and classic pipelines sharing the same resources

notes.front: A pipeline's pass rate has fallen to 70 per cent and the team wants to know which single task to fix first. Where should they look?
notes.choices:
A) The pool consumption report
B) The top failing tasks in the pipeline pass rate report
C) The pipeline duration report
D) The retention settings
notes.back: B) The top failing tasks in the pipeline pass rate report
notes.choicesExplained: A shows queueing against parallel jobs. C shows slow tasks, not failing ones. D controls how long runs are kept.
notes.explanation: The pass rate report lists the top failing tasks and their failed runs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Pipeline reports”, “Pipeline pass rate report” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Top failing tasks & their failed runs**: Lists the top failing tasks, their trend and provides pointers to their failed runs.

notes.front: Successful builds now take 40 minutes instead of 15. Which report shows the tasks responsible?
notes.back: The pipeline duration report, through its top tasks by duration.
notes.explanation: It shows the duration trend and the tasks taking the longest.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Pipeline reports”, “Pipeline duration report” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can review the duration trend and analyze the top tasks by duration to optimize the duration of the pipeline.

notes.front: Random test failures unrelated to code changes keep failing builds, and developers have started ignoring red builds. What should the team configure?
notes.choices:
A) Delete the failing tests
B) Add parallel jobs
C) Lower the retention period
D) Turn on flaky test management and choose to prevent build failures caused by flaky tests
notes.back: D) Turn on flaky test management and choose to prevent build failures caused by flaky tests
notes.choicesExplained: A loses test coverage. C and B do not change how test outcomes are treated.
notes.explanation: Flaky test management can stop flaky tests failing builds instead of only tagging them for troubleshooting.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage flaky tests”, “Enable flaky test management” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Report on flaky tests** - Ability to choose if you want to prevent build failures caused by flaky tests, or use the flaky tag only for troubleshooting

notes.front: Every run of a GitHub Actions workflow spends four minutes downloading the same npm packages on GitHub-hosted runners. What reduces this?
notes.choices:
A) A larger runner
B) Uploading the packages as a workflow artifact
C) Adding a concurrency group
D) Dependency caching of the npm cache
notes.back: D) Dependency caching of the npm cache
notes.choicesExplained: A adds power but still downloads every time. B is for passing files between jobs, not reusing dependencies across runs. C limits concurrent runs.
notes.explanation: Caching lets later runs reuse downloaded dependencies instead of fetching them again in a clean runner image.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Dependency caching”, “About workflow dependency caching”
notes.evidence: Workflow runs often reuse the same outputs or downloaded dependencies from one run to another.

notes.front: Developers complain that builds wait 20 minutes in the queue. How should you decide whether to buy more parallel jobs?
notes.choices:
A) Register more self-hosted agents without checking
B) Buy one parallel job per developer
C) Open the pool consumption report and look for queued jobs while running jobs are at the limit
D) Shorten retention
notes.back: C) Open the pool consumption report and look for queued jobs while running jobs are at the limit
notes.choicesExplained: B far exceeds the rule of thumb of one job per four to five users. A adds agents, but self-hosted concurrency is charged by parallel jobs, not agents. D affects storage, not queues.
notes.explanation: A backlog of queued jobs at the concurrency limit is the documented sign that more parallel jobs may be needed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Configure and pay for parallel jobs”, “View job history using the pool consumption report” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you have a backlog of queued jobs and your running jobs are at the concurrency limit, you might want to purchase more parallel jobs.

notes.front: Two pushes a minute apart start two production deployment workflows, which overwrite each other. What GitHub Actions feature prevents this?
notes.back: A concurrency group, using the `concurrency` keyword, so only one deployment runs at a time.
notes.explanation: Disabling concurrent execution is suggested precisely to stop multiple deployments running at once.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Concurrency”, “Concurrency”
notes.evidence: For example, you might want to prevent multiple deployments from running at the same time

notes.front: A multistage YAML pipeline must keep runs that deploy to production for two years, while test runs follow the normal 30-day policy. What should the production stage do?
notes.choices:
A) Set a per-pipeline retention policy
B) Configure retention on the production environment
C) Call the Lease API from a script to add a two-year retention lease on its run
D) Raise the project's retention to two years for everything
notes.back: C) Call the Lease API from a script to add a two-year retention lease on its run
notes.choicesExplained: A is no longer supported. B is not possible for YAML pipelines. D keeps every run far longer than needed.
notes.explanation: Leases can be set for a duration, such as longer for runs that deploy to production.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “Automatically set retention lease on pipeline runs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You can retain a run that deploys to production for a longer time.

notes.front: Storage is filling with pull request runs kept as long as main-branch runs. Where do you shorten how long pull request runs are kept?
notes.back: Project settings > Pipelines > Settings, by setting the days to keep pull request runs.
notes.explanation: That page sets separate day counts for runs and for pull request runs.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “Configure retention policies” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Set how many days to keep pull request runs.

notes.front: A build job produces test screenshots that a later reporting job in the same workflow must read, and testers want them after the run ends. What should the build job produce?
notes.choices:
A) A cache entry
B) A concurrency group
C) A retention lease
D) A workflow artifact
notes.back: D) A workflow artifact
notes.choicesExplained: A is for reusing dependencies across runs and should be treated as untrusted. C is an Azure Pipelines feature. B controls concurrent runs.
notes.explanation: Artifacts persist data after a job and share it with other jobs in the same workflow; screenshots are a listed common artifact.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Workflow artifacts”, “About workflow artifacts”
notes.evidence: * Test results, failures, and screenshots

notes.front: A team selects "Export to YAML" for its classic release pipeline but the option is missing. What is the documented way forward?
notes.choices:
A) Open a specific run and export from there
B) Export each task individually and rebuild the pipeline in YAML
C) Upgrade the agent pool
D) Enable flaky test management
notes.back: B) Export each task individually and rebuild the pipeline in YAML
notes.choicesExplained: A fails because the option appears only in the pipeline definition view, and release pipelines cannot export anyway. C and D do not affect export.
notes.explanation: Classic release pipelines do not support YAML export, so tasks are exported one by one.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Migrate your Classic pipeline to YAML”, “Migrate your Classic pipeline to YAML” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Classic release pipelines don’t support YAML export, you'll need to export each task individually.

notes.front: A security review wants every change to pipeline steps to go through pull request review, and no new Classic pipelines to appear. What should the organisation do?
notes.back: Migrate to YAML pipelines protected by branch policies, and disable the creation of classic build and release pipelines.
notes.explanation: YAML pipelines are defined in code and can be reviewed; creation of Classic pipelines can be disabled independently.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Secure your Azure Pipelines”, “Use YAML pipelines instead of Classic pipelines” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Disable creating Classic pipelines**: Independently disable the creation of classic build pipelines and classic release pipelines.

notes.front: Dependency caching versus workflow artifacts: what is each for?
notes.back: Caching: reusing downloaded dependencies across runs. Artifacts: keeping a run's output and passing it between jobs.
notes.explanation: Artifacts persist data after a job completes; caches speed up recreating files between runs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Workflow artifacts”, “About workflow artifacts”
notes.evidence: Artifacts allow you to persist data after a job has completed, and share that data with another job in the same workflow.

notes.front: Pipeline retention policy versus retention lease: what does each govern?
notes.back: Policy: project-wide rules for how long runs are kept. Lease: keeping a specific run beyond those rules.
notes.explanation: Leases extend or control a run's lifetime beyond the configured retention periods.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Retention policies”, “Automatically set retention lease on pipeline runs” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Retention leases let you extend or control the lifetime of pipeline runs beyond configured retention periods.
